{"url": "https://api.crossref.org/works?query=autonomous+inquiry+problem+formulation+curiosity+open+ended+learning+scientific+discovery&rows=4&select=DOI%2Ctitle%2Cabstract%2CURL%2Cpublished", "scope": "Crossref bibliographic metadata and abstracts where supplied; not full papers", "excerpt": "[{\"DOI\": \"10.31764/jtam.v4i1.1736\", \"title\": [\"Problem Based Learning, Discovery Learning, and Open Ended Models: An experiment On Mathematical Problem Solving Ability\"], \"abstract\": \"<jats:p>This research is to look at the effect of problem-based learning, discovery learning, and open-ended models on the mathematical problem-solving abilities of students. The type of research is a quasi-experiment with a three treatment counterbalanced design research design. The instruments used: (1) students 'initial mathematical ability tests, (2) tests of students' mathematical problem-solving abilities with the Pythagorean Theorem material. Inferential data were performed using covariance analysis (ANACOVA). The samples of this study were 32 students each from three experimental classes selected by purposive sampling. The results are: (1) of the three learning models conducted using the model of problem-based learning, discovery learning, and open-ended had a positive effect on the ability to solve mathematical problems; (2) the ability to solve mathematical problems of students taught by problem-based learning models is better than the using discovery learning and open-ended models; and (3) there is an interaction between the initial ability of mathematics and learning models.</jats:p>\", \"URL\": \"https://doi.org/10.31764/jtam.v4i1.1736\", \"published\": {\"date-parts\": [[2020, 4, 24]]}}, {\"DOI\": \"10.5040/9798216526087.ch02\", \"title\": [\"Creative and Innovative Thinking\"], \"URL\": \"https://doi.org/10.5040/9798216526087.ch02\", \"published\": {\"date-parts\": [[2013]]}}, {\"DOI\": \"10.1007/978-1-4614-7224-7_3\", \"title\": [\"Open-Ended Inquiry\"], \"URL\": \"https://doi.org/10.1007/978-1-4614-7224-7_3\", \"published\": {\"date-parts\": [[2013]]}}, {\"DOI\": \"10.3030/713010\", \"URL\": \"https://doi.org/10.3030/713010\"}]", "excerpt_truncated": false, "source_sha256": "7fcab16bc5f907214385eedde9a547e752878ebd5d71a609705b009dcdb1b39d", "verification_required": true, "topic_domain": "unassigned_problem", "evidence_role": "discovery", "host_tier": "discovery…

{"url": "https://www.ebi.ac.uk/europepmc/webservices/rest/search?query=philosophical+frameworks+of+moral+agency+autonomous+systems+accountability&format=json&resultType=core&pageSize=4", "scope": "Europe PMC search metadata, abstracts and full-text links; discovery only", "excerpt": "[{\"title\": \"Authorship responsibilities of scientists who use AI research agents.\", \"abstract\": \"The advent of artificial intelligence (AI) tools capable of performing research independently, which we call AI research agents (AIRAs) is likely to significantly impact how science is planned, performed, reviewed, evaluated, and communicated. However, the expected gains in efficiency and productivity from the deployment of AIRAs should not undermine science's epistemic and ethical values, such as accountability, transparency, reproducibility, and rigor. In this paper, we revisit the AI authorship debate in light of the reported capabilities of AIRAs and argue that these tools do not qualify for authorship because they cannot be held morally responsible for their contributions. We also reject the use of the term \\\"scientist\\\" to refer to these tools and argue that human scientists who use AIRAs have three key authorship responsibilities: (1) to carefully oversee and manage AIRAs; (2) to accurately and appropriately disclose AIRAs' contribution to research; and (3) to be accountable for research involving AIRAs by addressing questions and concerns raised by the scientific community and the public. Finally, we consider some related researcher responsibilities that are topics for future research, including the obligation to monitor, audit, and evaluate the performance of AIRAs and the obligation to address the social, economic, legal, and environmental implications of using AIRAs.\", \"doi\": \"10.3389/fgene.2026.1954843\", \"pmid\": \"42908681\", \"pmcid\": \"PMC13683075\", \"source\": \"MED\", \"fullTextUrlList\": {\"fullTextUrl\": [{\"availability\": \"Subscription required\", \"availabilityCode\": \"S\", \"documentStyle\": \"doi\", \"site\": \"DOI\", \"url\": \"https://doi.org/10.3389/fgene.2026.1954843\"}, {\"availability\": \"Open access\", \"availabilityCode\": \"OA\", \"documentStyle\": \"html\", \"site\": \"Europe_PMC\", \"url\": \"https://europepmc.org/articles/PMC13683075\"}, {\"availability\": \"Open access\", \"availabilityCode\": \"OA\", \"documentStyle\": \"pdf…

{"url": "https://arxiv.org/pdf/2609.32361v1.pdf", "scope": "bounded PDF text extraction from up to 24 pages; figures, tables, equations, layout, and scanned-image text may be incomplete", "excerpt": "Black-Box Auditing of Epistemic Reliability in
Multi-Agent Debate Distillation
Derui Wang1,* Zewei Shi1,2,*,† Rayne Holland1 Ruoxi Sun1 Xingliang Yuan2
Jason Xue1 Liming Zhu1
1CSIRO 2The University of Melbourne
Abstract
Debate distillation adapts weaker verifiers using multi-agent debate transcripts to improve their judge-
ment in subsequent debates, but gains on monitored tasks do not establish reliability on related
unmonitored tasks. We studyepistemic reliability degradation, in which adaptation preserves monitored
performance while reducing support for correct responses on hidden tasks. We consider an adversarial
debater that manipulates debate arguments while defending the correct monitored response, and
ask whether the resulting degradation merely reflects catastrophic forgetting and whether standard
evaluation can detect it. To address these questions, we proposeER-Audit, a two-stage black-box
auditing framework that compares frozen verifier checkpoints before and after adaptation, and introduce
two evaluation benchmarks pairing monitored and hidden task prompts grounded in shared contexts.
ER-Auditsearches for counterexamples to non-degradation by evaluating semantically valid para-
phrases and, if none is found, uses independent paraphrases for sequential hypothesis testing. We derive
anytime-valid lower confidence bounds on the non-degradation probability, allowing data-dependent
stopping within a finite budget. We further establish a common lower bound across fixed paraphrase
distributions and extend it to distributions within a bounded total variation distance of their mixtures.
Our experiments show that higher hidden-task accuracy can coexist with more counterexamples to
non-degradation and lower non-degradation bounds. This divergence challenges explanations based
solely on broad catastrophic forgetting and shows that auditing can uncover selective hidden-task degra-
dation concealed by aggregate performance gains. Our code and benchmarks are available athttps:
//github.com/CSIRO-CQS-AI-alignment-Team/Epistemic-Reliability-Auditor.
